# Median pairing transport: exact reduction and audited target laws

This note concerns `n=1`. It records a valid coupling reduction and obstructions to several natural target-law prescriptions. It does not prove the required existence of a suitable coupling.

## 1. Exact coupling lemma

Let `μ` be a probability measure on the mixed-integer set `S`, and let `z0` be a weighted median of its integer marginal. Thus the masses `L=μ{z<z0}` and `R=μ{z>z0}` are each at most `1/2`. The central fiber has mass `w=1−L−R`.

Split its measure into proportional submeasures of masses `1/2−L` and `1/2−R`. Together with the strict left and right measures, these yield submeasures `μ−,μ+` of mass `1/2`, supported in `z≤z0` and `z≥z0`, with `μ−+μ+=μ`.

Let `π` be any coupling of these submeasures, so its total mass is `1/2`. For a pair `p=(z−,x−), q=(z+,x+)` with `z−<z+`, define

`T(p,q) = (z0, [(z+−z0)x−+(z0−z−)x+]/(z+−z−))`.

If both indices equal `z0`, set `T(p,q)=(p+q)/2`. This is a Borel map, and its value lies in the selected fiber by convexity of `C`.

Define the probability law `ν=2 T#π` on that fiber. Then every closed ambient halfspace `H` satisfies

`μ(H) ≥ ν(H)/2`.

Indeed, if both endpoints lie outside the closed halfspace, their whole segment lies in its open convex complement. Therefore

`1_H(T(p,q)) ≤ 1_H(p)+1_H(q)`

pointwise, including when the image belongs to the boundary. Integrating proves the inequality by the marginal identities.

Consequently, if some coupling yields a law `ν` with one point of depth at least `γ_d`, the same point has original depth at least `γ_d/2`. The selected point automatically belongs to `S`. No rounding, orientation restriction, or boundary-mass exclusion is involved.

An arbitrary coupling gives only the ordinary continuous centerpoint bound `1/(d+1)` for its target law, recovering the mixed Helly factor. Thus the remaining issue is the existence of a coupling whose target law has the stronger sharp depth property.

## 2. Uniformity on a Minkowski average can be impossible

Even for two fixed source fibers, every coupling of uniform laws on `A,B⊂R^d` has the same midpoint mean `(c(A)+c(B))/2`. It therefore cannot be uniform on `(A+B)/2` unless that body's centroid has the required value.

For an explicit planar example, use

`A=conv{(0,0),(2,0),(0,2)}`, `B=[0,1]^2`.

Then `c(A)=(2/3,2/3)` and `c(B)=(1/2,1/2)`, so every midpoint law has mean `(7/12,7/12)`.

The Minkowski sum has vertices `(0,0),(3,0),(3,1),(1,3),(0,3)`. Its area is `7`, and its centroid is `(53/42,53/42)`: this follows by subtracting the top-right triangle of area `2` and centroid `(7/3,7/3)` from `[0,3]^2`. Thus uniform measure on the half-scaled sum has centroid `(53/84,53/84)`, different from `(7/12,7/12)`.

This rules out uniform Minkowski interpolation as a universal prescription. It does not rule out uniformity on a different target body, or a different target law with the desired depth.

## 3. Brenier interpolation need not preserve log-concavity

Quadratic optimal transport is not an automatic solution. Santambrogio and Wang prove that displacement interpolation between uniform measures on convex planar bodies can have nonconvex support, precluding log-concavity. Their primary paper is [Convexity of the support of the displacement interpolation: counterexamples](https://www.normalesup.org/~mfathi/docs/enseignement/articles%20TO%20M2/CounterexampleConvexity.pdf).

This was consulted solely as ordinary optimal-transport background, not as a search for the mixed-integer conjecture or its status.

## 4. Even simple independent pairing can lose log-concavity

Take the planar convex body with integer fibers at `z=−1,0,1` equal to `[0,1]`, `[0,1+ε]`, `[0,1]`, where `0<ε<1`; the concave upper boundary is the linear tent between those endpoints. Normalize mixed volume, whose total is `3+ε`.

Couple the two outer fibers independently, and couple the two halves of the central fiber diagonally. Under median intersection, the outer-pair contribution is the average of two independent `Unif[0,1]` variables; write its density as `g(x)=4x` for `0≤x≤1/2` and `g(x)=4(1−x)` for `1/2≤x≤1`.

The normalized target density is

`f(x)=[1+2g(x)]/(3+ε)` on `[0,1]`, and `f(x)=1/(3+ε)` on `(1,1+ε]`.

It is not log-concave: at the interior point `x=1`, the derivative of `log f` jumps upward from `−8` to `0`, whereas a concave function has nonincreasing one-sided derivatives. This does not refute a carefully chosen alternative coupling. It shows that independence plus the source body's convexity is not enough to assert the target-law property.

## Route status

The factor-two coupling inequality is proved. Uniform Minkowski interpolation, automatic Brenier log-concavity, and automatic independence log-concavity are each unavailable for exact reasons. A different coupling invariant that forces target depth `γ_d` remains unproved; it cannot be supplied by ordinary compactness alone.

## 5. Arbitrary coupling can fail the target depth itself

Let

`Z=conv{(0,0),(1,0),(2,1),(2,2),(1,2),(0,1)}`.

This area-three hexagon is the union, with disjoint interiors, of the three area-one parallelograms

```
Q1 = [0,1]^2
Q2 = (1,0) + [0,(0,1)] + [0,(1,1)]
Q3 = (0,1) + [0,(1,0)] + [0,(1,1)].
```

Reflect a uniform source point within whichever tile contains it. This is a measure-preserving pairing of two uniform laws on the same convex body `Z`. Its midpoint law consists of three equal atoms at the tile centers

`(1/2,1/2), (3/2,1), (1,3/2)`.

Those centers form a triangle, whose equally weighted atomic law has maximum halfspace depth `1/3`, below `γ_2=4/9`. The same tile reflection can be used for both the outer-fiber pairs and central-fiber pairs in `C=[−1,1]×Z`. Hence even the target depth property, rather than just log-concavity, is not automatic for a coupling of uniform convex marginals.

## 6. A large uniform component does not by itself suffice

Let `K` be any planar convex body with an exposed vertex `v`, and put

`ν=(2/3)Unif(K)+(1/3)δ_v`.

Its maximum halfspace depth is exactly `1/3`. At `v`, each containing halfspace carries the atom, and exposing caps with vanishing area show that its depth equals `1/3`.

For any point `y≠v`, a line through `y,v` has a side containing at most half the area of `K`. Rotate that side's boundary arbitrarily slightly about `y` so as to exclude `v`. The uniform masses converge to at most one half, while the atom is omitted. Thus the infimum of the corresponding halfspace masses is at most `(2/3)(1/2)=1/3`.

This obstruction cannot simply be inserted into the pairing construction with positive-volume endpoint fibers: the midpoint of their interior points is interior to their Minkowski average, so a collapsed endpoint law cannot occur at a boundary vertex of the containing central fiber. That is a precise geometric compatibility constraint an improved transport argument would have to exploit.
